title: Basic Feedback Analytics and Efficacy for Skill Formation
author: Alfred Essa
summary: Alfred Essa extends his earlier "Three Ironclad Laws of Skill Formation" (skills are habits, practice should be spaced, and progress is nonlinear) by asking what instructors and learners should measure once they accept those laws. He frames the instructor as an empirical coach who needs minimal, transparent data about practice sessions: what activities build the skill, how often to practice, and how to space and size the sessions. He illustrates the idea with a Spanish-reading application and a simple weekly dashboard that shows practice rhythm and lets students set their own goals. He argues that this basic practice data can seed efficacy studies, since single-shot randomized trials are not enough for science to advance. Throughout he positions the frontline instructor, not a generic AI tutor, as the person who designs experiments and judges results. He closes with Orwell on scientific education as a method of thinking rather than a pile of facts.
points: Skill formation depends on habit, spacing and plateaus, so learning technology should be judged by whether it supports regular, spread-out practice rather than by how clever it is.
Start analytics with the absolute minimum data (what was practiced, how often, how long), applying an Occam's Razor for data analytics and keeping collection transparent to learners.
A minimal dashboard showing daily practice and learner-set goals gives both student and coach the feedback that turns plain practice into deliberate practice.
Baseline practice data lets instructors pose concrete efficacy questions, such as whether students practicing three times a week for 15 to 30 minutes outperform peers on the first exam.
AI can assist, but the frontline instructor must frame hypotheses and judge the experiments, because the right training design cannot be known in advance for each cohort.
quotes: Athletes and their coaches know the three laws in their bones. Runners don’t become runners by watching running videos. Nor do they turn to AI to do their running for them.

Becoming “AI literate” is also of no use whatsoever for a beginner. There is no magical fairy dust, not even AI fairy dust, that we can sprinkle on ourselves as a substitute for good old-fashioned effort and practice.
DATA is important, but we should not get carried away. Here we can apply Occam’s Razor for Data Analytics: begin with the absolute minimum; don’t let data multiply without justification
The answers to the three questions above cannot be known a priori, AI or no AI. It takes experience and experimentation to calibrate the right training for each cohort and for each student.
The problem with most efficacy studies, even “rigorous” ones using Randomized Control Trials (RCTs), is that they are single-shot. Science does not advance based on single experiments.

The point is that typically the instructor, along with support from learning designers, is in the best position to frame hypotheses, establish experiments, collect data, evaluate the results, and set up the next round of experiments. AI can help, but the frontline instructor has to be the judge and design the experiments.

Clearly, scientific education ought to mean the implanting of a rational, skeptical, experimental habit of mind. It ought to mean acquiring a method — a method that can be used on any problem that one meets — and not simply piling up a lot of facts.
